Q1 compares the menus of two bars pair‐wise: it returns a pair (b1, b2) if every beer that b1 serves is also served by b2 but b2 serves at least one beer that b1 does not. In contrast, Q2 starts from the Serves table by joining two rows with different bars and then uses a subquery (with a LEFT JOIN that is not correlated to the outer query) whose result is independent of the pair (b1,b2). In our counterexample the subquery in Q2 returns no row (so its NOT EXISTS condition is satisfied), and the join produces duplicate rows (multiplicity) that differ from Q1’s single result. Thus the two queries produce different outputs over the same data.
counterexample_dsp: Two bars A and B are inserted along with two beers x and y. Bar A serves only beer x, while bar B serves beers x and y. Q1 returns the pair (A,B) because A's menu is a strict subset of B's. Q2, however, returns two duplicate rows (because of its join on serves) even though its subquery is satisfied. This difference in multiplicity (and possibly in semantics) serves as a counterexample.

Bar1ServesBeer AS (
	SELECT bar1, count1, s.beer AS beer1
	FROM Bar1ServesCount AS b1 INNER JOIN serves AS s
	ON b1.bar1=s.bar

Bar2ServesBeer AS (
	SELECT bar2, count2, s.beer AS beer2
	FROM Bar2ServesCount AS b2 INNER JOIN serves AS s
	ON b2.bar2=s.bar

	FROM Bar2ServesBeer AS b2 LEFT JOIN Bar1ServesBeer AS b1
	ON b2.beer2=b1.beer1
	AND b2.bar2<>b1.bar1
	AND b2.count2>b1.count1
	WHERE b1.bar1 IS NOT NULL AND b1.beer1 IS NOT NULL
)
